espresso.what: Hot water forced through a compacted bed of fine coffee at around 9 bar. Everything happens in half a minute, which is why every variable matters so much.
steps: Grind fine and dose into a dry, level basket.
Distribute — WDT with a needle tool breaks up clumps that would otherwise channel.
Tamp level. Pressure matters less than being flat; a tilted puck extracts unevenly.
Lock in and start the shot immediately. A hot puck sitting in the group starts extracting before the pump does.
Watch the first drops: 5–10 seconds before flow is normal. Under 3 means too coarse, over 15 means too fine.
Stop at your target yield by weight, not by eye.

faults.cause: Under-extracted. Grind finer or raise the dose.
Over-extracted. Grind coarser, lower the temperature, or shorten the shot.

faults.symptom: Fast then slow, tastes both sour and bitter
faults.cause: Channelling. Water found a crack and skipped most of the puck. Better distribution, not a finer grind.
Far too fine, or over-dosed for the basket.

gear.what: A single-boiler machine with a decent portafilter, plus a hand grinder. The grinder matters more than the machine — a great machine cannot fix an uneven grind.
Heat exchanger or dual boiler for temperature stability, and a flat-burr electric grinder. This is where shot-to-shot consistency arrives.
Multi-boiler with PID and pressure profiling, on-demand commercial grinder. Buys repeatability across hundreds of shots a day, not a better single shot.

notes: 58 mm is the commercial standard basket; 51 and 54 mm appear on smaller home machines and hold less coffee.

Pressurised (dual-wall) baskets create back-pressure artificially, so they forgive a bad grinder but flatten the flavour and cannot be dialled in. Non-pressurised (single-wall) baskets reward a good grinder and are what you want once you have one.

coneDripper.what: A conical dripper with a large single hole — V60, Origami, Kono. You control the flow with your pour, which is what makes it expressive and unforgiving.
steps: Rinse the paper filter with hot water; it removes papery taste and preheats the brewer.
Add grounds, level the bed, and make a small well in the centre.
Bloom with two to three times the dose in water. Wait 30–45 seconds while it degasses.
Pour in slow spirals from the centre outward, keeping the bed level.
Aim for 3–5 pours. Finish with a gentle swirl to flatten the bed.
Drawdown should finish shortly after the last pour.

faults.symptom: Drains far too fast, tastes thin
faults.cause: Too coarse, or you poured too aggressively and broke the bed.

faults.symptom: Stalls, takes far too long, bitter
faults.cause: Too fine, or fines migrated and blocked the filter.

faults.symptom: Grounds high on the wall when finished
faults.cause: Uneven pouring. Those grounds never got extracted.

gear.what: A plastic V60 (holds heat better than glass), paper filters, and any kettle you can pour slowly from.
Gooseneck kettle with temperature control, and a burr grinder. The kettle changes pour control more than the dripper does.
Scale with built-in timer and flow readout. Mostly about repeating a recipe exactly.

notes: Origami on a cone filter behaves like a V60; on a wave filter it behaves flat-bottomed.
Kono's ribs stop short of the top, so the paper seals against the wall and flow slows — expect longer times than a V60.

flatBottomDripper.what: A flat bed with small restricted holes — Kalita Wave, Stagg [X], Orea, April. The flat bed extracts more evenly than a cone, so it is more forgiving of an imperfect pour.
steps: Rinse the filter and preheat.
Add grounds and level the bed — flat means flat here, it matters more than on a cone.
Bloom with two to three times the dose, 30–45 seconds.
Pour in gentle concentric circles, avoiding the wall.
Keep the water level fairly constant rather than letting it drain fully between pours.

faults.cause: Too fine — the restricted holes clog more readily than a cone's.
Too coarse, or the bed drained dry between pours.

gear.what: Kalita Wave 155 in stainless, and its wave filters.
Add a gooseneck kettle and a decent grinder. Orea or April if you want faster flow and more control.
Batch-consistent filters and a flow-measuring scale.

notes: Kalita's three small holes restrict flow by design, so it runs longer than a cone. That is not a fault to correct.
Wave filters are dearer and less widely stocked than cone papers — worth checking before you commit.

chemex.what: A conical brewer with a filter roughly three times the thickness of a normal paper. That filter is the whole point: it strips oils and fines, giving an unusually clean, tea-like cup.
steps: Rinse the filter thoroughly — the thick paper carries a lot of taste. Put the triple-fold side over the spout.
Add grounds coarser than you would for a V60.
Bloom 30–45 seconds.
Pour slowly in the centre, avoiding the wall where the filter folds.
Expect a longer total time than any other pour-over. That is correct, not slow.

faults.cause: Too fine. A Chemex clogs earlier than a V60 because the paper is thicker.
The filter was not rinsed enough.
Too coarse — long contact with coarse coffee still under-extracts.

gear.what: A 6-cup Chemex and its bonded filters. Nothing else fits properly.
Gooseneck kettle and a grinder that can go coarse without producing fines.
Little to add — the Chemex is already the simple end of the craft.

notes: A three-minute Chemex is fast, not normal. Judge it against 3:30–4:30.
The thick filter is why a Chemex tastes cleaner and lighter-bodied than a V60 with the same coffee.

batchBrewer.what: A machine that heats and doses the water for you. You control the grind and the ratio; it controls everything else.
steps: Use a ratio around 1:16 and weigh both coffee and water — the carafe markings are usually optimistic.
Grind medium, roughly like table salt.
Check the machine reaches 92–96 °C. Many cheap brewers do not, and that is the single biggest cause of weak coffee.
Pull the carafe as soon as it finishes; a hotplate cooks coffee bitter within minutes.

faults.symptom: Weak and sour no matter what
faults.cause: The machine is not getting hot enough. No grind change fixes this.
The hotplate. Decant into a thermos instead.
The showerhead is not wetting the bed evenly — a known weakness on cheaper machines.

gear.what: Any brewer that actually hits temperature. Certification by a coffee body is a reasonable shortcut.
A brewer with a proper showerhead, pre-infusion, and a thermal carafe rather than a hotplate.
Commercial batch brewer with programmable pulse profiles and a heated dispenser.

notes: There are no bloom or pour fields for this method because the machine decides them. Score what you control.

aeropress.what: Immersion plus pressure through a paper filter. Forgiving, fast, and almost impossible to make undrinkable — which is why it travels so well.
steps: Rinse the filter and assemble. Upright is simpler; inverted lets you steep without drips.
Add coffee, then water. Stir gently to wet everything.
Steep 60–120 seconds.
Press slowly and evenly — 20–30 seconds. If it presses in five, the grind is too coarse.
Stop pressing when you hear air. Pushing further pulls bitterness through.

faults.cause: Too fine. Uncomfortable to push and usually bitter.
Too coarse.
You pressed past the hiss.

gear.what: An AeroPress and paper filters. That is genuinely the whole kit.
A hand grinder and a scale. A metal filter if you want more body and less clarity.
Nothing meaningful. The AeroPress does not scale up, which is part of its charm.

notes: Lower temperatures than other methods work well here — 80–85 °C suits light roasts and reduces bitterness.
The concentrate style (1:5, then diluted) is a different drink from a full-immersion 1:15. Both are valid; decide which you are making before judging it.

frenchPress.what: Full immersion with a metal mesh. The mesh lets oils and fine particles through, which is exactly what gives it that heavy body.
steps: Preheat the press. Coarse grind, like breadcrumbs.
Add all the water at once and stir the crust after a minute.
Steep four minutes total.
Skim the foam and floating grounds off the top before plunging — this removes most of the bitterness people blame on the method.
Plunge slowly and pour immediately. Coffee left on the grounds keeps extracting.

faults.cause: Grind too fine, or you plunged hard and forced fines through.
It sat on the grounds. Decant everything as soon as you plunge.
Ratio too lean, or steeped too briefly.

gear.what: Any press and a kettle. The most forgiving brewer there is.
A burr grinder — fines are the enemy here, and a blade grinder makes nothing but.
A double-walled steel press for heat retention, and a cupping spoon for skimming.

notes: Skimming rather than plunging hard is the single biggest improvement most people can make.

coldBrew.what: Coarse coffee steeped in cold water for many hours. Low temperature extracts very little acidity, which is why it tastes sweet and soft rather than bright.
steps: Grind coarse. Fines turn cold brew muddy and there is no filter fast enough to save it.
Combine at roughly 1:8 for a concentrate, 1:15 to drink straight.
Stir to wet everything, then leave it. Room temperature 12–16 hours, or in the fridge 16–24.
Strain through a paper filter or a cloth. Expect it to take a while.
Keep refrigerated and drink within a week.

faults.cause: Too coarse, too short, or the ratio was too lean.
Too fine, or you squeezed the grounds while straining.
Left too long at room temperature. Move it to the fridge.

gear.what: A jar and a paper filter. Nothing else is required.
A dedicated brewer with a fine mesh basket, and fridge space.
Nitro tap and kegs, which is a serving question rather than a brewing one.

notes: A hot bloom — wetting the grounds with a little hot water first — brings out more aroma before the long cold steep. Worth trying; there is a field for it.

turkishIbrik.what: Coffee ground to a powder, boiled with the water, and served without filtering. The grounds settle in the cup rather than being removed, which makes it a decoction rather than an immersion.
steps: Grind finer than espresso — it should feel like flour.
Combine coffee, cold water and any sugar in the ibrik before heating. Sugar goes in now, never after.
Heat slowly. Do not stir once it warms.
As foam rises, lift it off the heat before it boils over. Traditionally repeated two or three times.
Pour gently, foam first, and let it settle a minute before drinking.

faults.cause: Heated too fast, or the grind is not fine enough.
Poured too quickly, or not left to settle.
It actually boiled. It should never reach a rolling boil.

gear.what: A copper or brass ibrik and a grinder that can reach powder — most burr grinders cannot.
A dedicated Turkish mill, usually a hand mill built for this fineness.
A sand-bed heater, which heats far more evenly than a flame.

notes: Closest relative among the other methods is kopi tubruk — both leave the grounds in the cup.

smartDripper.what: A dripper with a valve — Clever, Hario Switch. You steep like a French press, then release it through a paper filter. Immersion body with pour-over clarity.
steps: Rinse the filter with the valve closed.
Add grounds and all the water at once. Stir to wet.
Steep two to four minutes — this is where extraction happens, not during the drain.
Open the valve (or set it on the cup) and let it draw down.
The drawdown should take under a minute. Longer means too fine.

faults.cause: Too fine, or fines have blocked the paper.
Too coarse. Steep time cannot rescue a grind that is too big.

gear.what: A Clever dripper and standard cone filters.
A Hario Switch, which lets you alternate steeping and percolating within one brew.
Not a café brewer, but excellent for tasting several coffees side by side.

notes: Because extraction happens during the steep, grind affects taste less here than in a pour-over — which makes it a forgiving place to start.

siphon.what: Vapour pressure pushes water into an upper chamber, it brews there, and a vacuum pulls it back down through a filter as it cools. Theatrical, and genuinely very clean.
steps: Fill the lower bulb with hot water to save time, and seat the filter in the upper chamber.
Bring to the boil; the water rises on its own.
Add coffee once the water is up. Stir gently to wet.
Brew 60–90 seconds, with a second gentle stir.
Remove the heat. The vacuum pulls it down in around 30 seconds — a good draw looks like a whirlpool.

faults.cause: Too fine, or the filter is clogged.

faults.symptom: Water rises before you are ready
faults.cause: Normal — just heat more gently.
Too coarse, or too short in the upper chamber.

gear.what: A 3-cup siphon and a butane burner. Cloth filters need proper care.
A halogen beam heater, which is far easier to control than a flame.
A multi-station siphon bar. Almost entirely about presentation.

notes: Cloth filters give the cleanest cup but must be kept wet in the fridge and replaced often. Paper and metal are easier.

kopiTubruk.what: Indonesian home coffee: fine grounds and sugar in the glass, boiling water poured over, and you wait for it to settle. No filter, no equipment.
steps: Put fine grounds and sugar straight into the glass.
Pour water just off the boil.
Stir once, then leave it alone.
Wait four to five minutes for the grounds to sink.
Drink from the top and stop before the sludge.

faults.cause: Not settled long enough, or stirred again after settling.
Water at a full boil, or left far too long before drinking.

gear.what: A glass and a kettle. That is the entire method, and it is why it is everywhere.
A grinder, so you can use fresh single-origin instead of pre-ground blends.
Not a café method, though some specialty shops serve it to make a point.

notes: Sugar traditionally goes in before the water, which helps it dissolve and slightly changes the extraction.

kopiSaring.what: Coffee brewed and strained through a cloth sock, common across Indonesia and Malaysia. The cloth holds back grounds while letting oils through, so it sits between filter and immersion.
steps: Rinse the sock in hot water — a dry cloth tastes of cloth.
Add fine grounds to the sock and set it in the pot.
Pour hot water through slowly.
Pour the result back through a second time for a stronger cup — this is the traditional 'tarik' idea.
Rinse the sock immediately after and store it wet, in the fridge if you brew daily.

faults.cause: The sock. Old coffee oils go rancid in cloth faster than anywhere else.
Water passed too quickly. Pour slower, or pass it twice.

gear.what: A cloth sock and a pot. Buy two so one is always clean.
A dedicated pouring kettle and several socks in rotation.
Standard kit in a warung, where the sock is used continuously and rinsed constantly.

notes: Cloth care is the whole method. A neglected sock ruins good coffee more reliably than any grind error.

kopiJoss.what: Yogyakarta street coffee: a glowing lump of charcoal dropped straight into the glass. The charcoal neutralises some acidity and adds a distinct smoky note.
steps: Brew a strong tubruk-style coffee with sugar.
Heat a lump of hardwood charcoal until it glows right through.
Knock the ash off, then drop it into the glass. It will hiss and foam hard.
Leave the charcoal in for about a minute, then lift it out.
Let it settle before drinking.

faults.cause: The charcoal was not fully glowing, or the ash was not knocked off.
The charcoal cooled too fast, or came out too soon.

gear.what: Hardwood charcoal only — never briquettes, which contain binders you should not drink.
Tongs and a small brazier.
A street cart with a permanent charcoal fire, which is where it belongs.

notes: Use lump hardwood charcoal, not barbecue briquettes. Briquettes are bound with additives that are not food-safe.

kopiTalua.what: Minangkabau egg coffee. A raw yolk is whipped with sugar until pale and thick, then strong coffee is poured over it, leaving a foam layer on top.
steps: Whip a raw egg yolk with sugar until pale, thick and roughly doubled — two to three minutes of hard work.
Brew strong coffee separately.
Pour the hot coffee slowly over the whipped yolk without stirring it in.
The foam should sit on top. Some add cinnamon or nutmeg.
Drink through the foam rather than mixing it.

faults.cause: Coffee too hot or poured too fast. Slow down.
The yolk was not whipped long enough.
Not enough sugar, or the egg was not fresh.

gear.what: A whisk and a strong arm. A milk frother works too.
An electric hand whisk, which makes the texture far more consistent.
Served in Padang restaurants, whipped to order.

notes: This uses raw egg. Use very fresh eggs, and skip it if you are pregnant or immunocompromised.

kopiKhop.what: From Aceh: the glass is served upside down on a saucer, and you drink the coffee as it seeps out, through a straw. The inverted glass keeps it hot for a remarkably long time.
steps: Brew strong coffee and pour it into a small glass.
Cover the glass with a saucer and invert the whole thing in one movement.
Lift the glass slightly so a little coffee escapes onto the saucer.
Drink from the saucer with a straw, or sip directly.
The seal keeps it hot far longer than an open cup.

faults.cause: The flip was hesitant. It has to be one confident motion.
The seal is too good — tilt the glass very slightly.

gear.what: A small thick glass and a flat saucer. The glass must have a smooth rim to seal.
Nothing to add; the method is the equipment.
Served across West Aceh, where the flip is done with practised speed.

notes: Grounds stay in the glass, which is part of why it works — they are held against the saucer.
